# Draft:Italian conquest of Somalia

Background
Demographics and Political Context
At the end of the 19th century, Somalia was inhabited principally by two main groups of Cushitic origin: the Galla and the Somalis. The Galla had at some earlier, indeterminate period imposed themselves upon the Bantu-origin tribes who had previously occupied the Juba Valley. The Somalis, in turn, had imposed themselves upon the Galla around the mid-19th century.
During the prolonged wars to push the Galla southwestward toward the Tana Valley (in present-day Kenya), the various Somali tribes and clans had frequently engaged in internecine conflict over the possession of the most fertile lands, thereby compounding an already intricate network of feuds that further strained inter-tribal relations.
To these two groups was added a substantial Arab population, which had settled along the coast in connection with the flourishing trade conducted aboard dhows (the traditional sailing vessels of the Indian Ocean) between the Somali littoral and the Persian Gulf, exploiting the regularity of the monsoon winds. It was the Arabs who introduced Sunni Islam among the local populations and provided the initial impetus for the development of Mogadishu, an impetus that was later arrested by the continuous infiltration of Somali tribes, who in the eighteenth century definitively occupied the city, after which it declined.
These warlike populations, mutually hostile and resistant to foreign presence, long frustrated the colonising attempts of European powers, including Portugal and Britain. Even Egypt, after nominally declaring its possession of the Somali coast and extending its dominion to Aden (1871–75), failed in its attempt to establish garrisons at Brava and Kismayo and was ultimately repelled.
By the close of the 19th century, the Islamic Sultanate of Zanzibar maintained garrisons along the stretch of coast known as the Benadir, to which ivory and slaves were conveyed from the interior. The principal ethnic groups of the Benadir were the Geledi, the Wa'daan, the Bimaal, and the Murusade. The Wa'daan and the Bimaal in particular were fiercely opposed to the settlement of non-Muslims in the region. Resistance to foreign encroachment was thus motivated not primarily by ethnic or economic considerations, but by religious ones.
Italian Ambitions
Italian interest in the Somali Peninsula and East Africa dates back to 1885, when Captain Antonio Cecchi was sent on a mission to explore potential sites for Italian emigration along the southern Somaliland coast. This early initiative was driven by the Italian Foreign Minister Mancini, whose ambitions included expanding Italy's territorial presence beyond Eritrea, which had been occupied in February 1885.
The results of this expedition, however, fell considerably short of expectations. He sailed to Zanzibar on the ship Barbarigo, where he had an audience with Sultan Sayyid Barghash. Cecchi soon discovered that the Sultan was already under the strong influence of representatives from other European powers, first through a Franco-British declaration in 1862, and later by growing German ambitions, and was unwilling to grant further concessions. Despite this failure, Italy and Zanzibar signed a commercial treaty in 1885 which guaranteed mutual freedom of trade and applied the most-favoured-nation principle. The treaty also provided for the exchange of consular representatives between the two parties.
Cecchi envisioned a grand strategy: connecting Massawa on the Red Sea to the mouth of the Jubba River through a vast Italian-controlled corridor that would both absorb Italian emigration and cement a major East African colony. Although Mancini judged this unrealistic, Cecchi persisted, and his ideas later found an eager supporter in Vincenzo Filonardi, the Italian consul in Zanzibar.
Filonardi repeatedly claimed, often dubiously, that the Sultan was prepared to cede Kismayo and the Jubba region to Italy, and he used every diplomatic incident, including a perceived slight to King Umberto I of Italy, to demand these concessions as "reparation". His aggressive posture, driven partly by personal commercial interests, sharply worsened relations with Zanzibar and alarmed Britain and Germany. Yet Filonardi remained committed to Cecchi's expansionist vision, urging military pressure and even seizure of customs revenues to force a cession.
Ultimately, neither Cecchi's aspirations nor Filonardi's forceful tactics succeeded: international politics, British protectorate control over Zanzibar (1890), and the Sultan's resistance ensured that Italy’s ambitions in Kismayo and the Jubba remained blocked for decades, with real territorial acquisition arriving only in the 1924–1925 Anglo-Italian agreement.
